 Etude India faces pricing challenge; looks beyond metros to grow K-beauty
 Korean beauty brand Etude is focusing on its complexion portfolio in India, aiming to balance K-beauty innovation and skincare-led products with competitive pricing in a value-conscious market.
 By   Chehneet Kaur | October 26, 2026, 14:00:52 IST Share Share this Article
 × WhatsApp Facebook Twitter Linkedin Mail 
 Follow Us 
 As more Korean beauty brands seek to capitalise on the same cultural momentum, familiarity with K-beauty may help consumers discover products, but differentiation will become increasingly important, as per Cho. India’s growing appetite for Korean beauty products is opening up opportunities for international brands, but translating the popularity of K-pop and K-dramas into sustained beauty consumption requires more than cultural familiarity.
 For Etude, the Korean makeup brand, the next phase of growth in India will depend on how effectively it brings its skincare-led approach to complexion products to a market where consumers weigh novelty against price.
 The brand is looking to establish its complexion portfolio in India, with a focus on products that combine makeup with skincare actives. It is also preparing new innovations specifically for the Indian market as it seeks to understand local consumer needs and communicate the benefits of Korean beauty to Indian buyers.
 “First, we need to make the success with our complexion products. And then for the next year, we’re actually preparing some exciting new innovations specifically for India as well,” Soye Cho, Head of Global Brand Marketing, Etude, Amorepacific group, told Storyboard18.

 From K-pop appeal to product differentiation 
 Korean beauty’s growing visibility has coincided with the international popularity of K-pop and Korean entertainment. Cho believes the aesthetics associated with Korean music and celebrities have helped introduce consumers to Korean beauty routines and products.
 “I think it first started with the K-pop culture, especially with all the singers, BTS and everyone. And then from there, you see their aesthetics. I think it’s spreading over the global market,” she said.
 For beauty brands, however, cultural interest is only one part of the equation. The task is to convert that interest into a reason to purchase a particular product.
 Etude’s approach centres on developing products with a clearly identifiable point of difference and building communication around that attribute. Cho, who oversees marketing communication for Korea as well as global product development, said the brand considers a product’s potential to generate conversation during the development process itself.
 “The product has to have this edge that could go viral. So we really try to think, what could be the nickname of this product? What could be the edge of this product? And then we try to use that same, consistent message so that it delivers to the consumers as well,” she said.
 The strategy puts product differentiation ahead of communication alone. Rather than relying solely on influencer visibility or media exposure, Etude wants consumers to recognise a distinctive product attribute and understand its value.
 The pricing challenge in a value-conscious market 
 For Etude, one of the central questions is how to preserve the appeal of Korean beauty innovation while competing in India’s price-sensitive cosmetics market.
 Cho acknowledged that the brand is aware of the price gap between its products and those offered by local brands. It is attempting to maintain competitive pricing while positioning its Korean beauty expertise as a reason for consumers to consider its products.
 “Right now, what we’re trying to do is we really want to have a competitive pricing in the Indian market,” she said, adding that Etude had historically been positioned in Korea as a brand consumers could buy easily and experiment with.
 “We’re fully aware that we’re a bit more expensive than local brands, but it’s because we do have the K-beauty edge, which we can offer, which we can bring something new to the Indian market,” Cho said.
 That positioning presents a balancing act. Pricing products too far above local alternatives could restrict the audience for a brand seeking to expand, while the cost of developing new formulations and innovations can make affordability difficult to achieve.
 Cho also drew a distinction between consumer behaviour in Korea and India. In Korea, she said, novelty itself can contribute to a product’s perceived luxury, encouraging consumers to try new launches.
 “In Korea, right now, I think the luxuriousness of this product comes from novelty. So whatever something new, whatever we offer new, they consider it and they just buy it,” she said.
 In India, she believes, novelty alone is unlikely to justify a higher price.
 “I cannot just offer something new with a high pricing. I mean, it’s not a strategy to, I guess, spread in the Indian market. So we really try to think what’s the edge that we could offer within this pricing and as a K-beauty makeup brand,” Cho said.
 Why complexion is the next focus 
 Etude’s immediate priority is to establish its complexion products, including its foundation range, in a market that already has offerings from domestic and international beauty brands.
 Cho said Korean beauty’s global growth was initially driven largely by skincare, with the opportunity now extending to makeup products that incorporate skincare benefits.
 “K-beauty spread with skincare, and none of the makeup brands really had a great appearance in the global market. So what we brought was the idea to bring these hybrid products into the Indian market,” she said.
 She sees the integration of skincare actives into complexion products as a key point of differentiation for Etude.
 “There are many foundations from local brands as well as overseas, foreign brands in the Indian market. But what K-beauty can bring is the actual purity of skin-caring actives inside a complexion product. So that’s what we bring as an edge,” Cho said.
 The proposition is to offer consumers makeup that also incorporates skin-focused ingredients, building on the association Korean beauty has developed with skincare routines and formulations. Whether that distinction can translate into sustained demand will depend on how clearly the brand communicates the benefits and how its products are priced against competing foundations.
 Etude is also looking beyond India’s largest urban markets. Cho said the brand has products across different price points, ranging from accessible offerings to products she described as more professional, which could serve consumers in tier-two and tier-three cities as well as larger urban centres.
 The reach of digital content could help expand that opportunity by exposing more consumers to Korean beauty trends and products.
 “Right now, it’s globalised, where you see all the content, K-pop content and everywhere, all the YouTube, TikTok, whatever. So I think we really have a chance to spread in India,” she said.
 Cho did not share a specific distribution plan, sales target or expansion timeline for these cities.
 Translating Korean beauty for Indian consumers 
 The next stage of growth will require a more localised understanding of consumer demand, rather than relying on the broader popularity of Korean entertainment and lifestyle.
 Cho said her team was working to understand Indian consumers and identify products that could meet their needs. The cost of innovation remains a central challenge, particularly when the brand is trying to offer new formulations at competitive prices.
 “Usually innovations are expensive. How do we offer this innovation with competitive pricing? That’s always the question I always have in my mind and always the challenges that I face with my brand presence,” she said.
 She added that the brand needs to communicate the benefits of Korean beauty in terms that Indian consumers can relate to.
 As more Korean beauty brands seek to capitalise on the same cultural momentum, familiarity with K-beauty may help consumers discover products, but differentiation will become increasingly important.
 For Etude, the immediate task is to establish its complexion portfolio, while its longer-term plans include new products developed specifically for India. The brand has not disclosed details of those launches, but Cho indicated that local consumer needs would remain central to the process.
 The opportunity lies in moving beyond the cultural appeal of Korean beauty to demonstrate why its products merit a place in Indian consumers’ routines and budgets. For a brand that acknowledges it can be more expensive than local alternatives, growth will depend on product differentiation, accessible pricing and a clearer articulation of what K-beauty offers.
